newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian firms earnings seen picking up next year.
newsitem.headline: Indian firms earnings seen picking up next year.

text.p: Indian companies are likely to boost their earnings next year as global commodity prices improve, the brokerage James Capel B&K said on Friday.
"While earnings growth will slow to 11 percent in FY97, we are forecasting a 23 percent growth in FY98 (1997/98 April-March)," the firm said in a report.
"This is because most of the factors affecting earnings in FY97 will have a one-time effect on the margins and...will bounce back as volumes jump."
Depressed world prices for petrochemicals, aluminium, steel and paper and lower import duties will squeeze margins of domestic firms this year, it said.

Steep increases in state-controlled prices of petroleum products, which pushed up input costs and freight charges across the board, and a minimum alternate tax (MAT) on companies were other factors that dimmed profit growth in fiscal 1996/97.
The brokerage said companies that had major expansion plans would be the hardest hit by the new tax.
The MAT, passed by parliament on Thursday, is aimed at high-growth firms that avoid paying taxes by ploughing profits back into new projects or expansions.

"Sectors such as petrochemicals, chemicals, paper and steel...will show negative earnings growth this year," it said. "It is only because of sectors such as automobiles, consumer goods and banks that the average earnings growth is still in double digits."
James Capel said its forecast for 1997/98 could be affected if companies changed their expansion plans due to liquidity problems. World commodity prices would also have a decisive say in the rebound.
"Our global house view is that most of these commodities should bounce back, which will have an overall positive impact on earnings," the report said.
The broking firm sees a selective market as valuations were not cheap.

"Although the market price/earnings multiples appear low, if we take into account the slowdown in earnings this year, a vulnerable next year and the high long-term interest rates, the valuations are not as cheap as they appear," it said.

James Capel said latent demand for capital would act as a dampener to the markets. Implementation of share depositories that would erase cumbersome physical share transfers, and lower long-term interest rates were likely to help an upturn.
"Till then, we feel that supply will exceed demand and the markets will remain sluggish -- a good opportunity to pick long-term winners," it said.
